planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; in the wild this species often grows as a lithophyte on rock faces, so it tolerates leaner, drier footing than most Cyrtomium.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown starts in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in part sun to light shade. Cyrtomium lonchitoides is a compact Chinese holly fern native to rocky forest slopes at 4,000-8,500 feet across several provinces, where it typically roots directly into stone crevices rather than deep soil, giving it unusual tolerance for lean, dry footing once established. Its low, dense evergreen clumps of glossy leaflets work well as a textural groundcover tucked into a rock garden, dry shaded border, or raised bed. It is notably deer- and rabbit-resistant and tolerates coastal salt exposure better than most ferns, making it a useful small-scale substitute where larger holly ferns would overwhelm the space.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; forms an unusually upright, structured vase of fronds rather than a loose arching clump.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade. This selection of Fortune's holly fern traces to spores collected along a Chinese roadside near 4,000 feet elevation and was later introduced through Plant Delights/Juniper Level Botanic Garden for its distinctly upright, vase-shaped habit, holding its very glossy, dark green fronds in a tidy structured clump that keeps its form through winter rather than flattening out like typical Cyrtomium fortunei. It is deer-resistant, tolerates short dry spells and coastal salt exposure once established, and makes a bolder architectural accent than the species for a shaded entry bed or foundation planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade; forms a tight, upright clump of thick, glossy fronds.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part sun to light shade. Selected and named from Chinese nursery stock, this compact Fortune's holly fern selection carries thick, glossy, dark green leaflets packed tightly along upright fronds, giving a denser, more congested silhouette than the wild species. It stays evergreen through mild winters, resists deer and rabbit browsing, and tolerates brief dry spells once established, making it a reliable mid-height texture plant for a shaded border, rain garden margin, or cottage-style planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; low, fine-textured clump with narrow leaflets distinct from broader-leaved forms of the species.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade. Collected from a high-elevation (about 4,700 feet) population of Fortune's holly fern near Tao Yuan in China, this low-growing selection is distinguished by notably narrower leaflets each marked with a dark central vein, giving the dense evergreen clump a finer, airier texture than typical, broader-leaved Cyrtomium fortunei. Its compact, low stature suits the front of a shaded border, a trough, or a small container where the wild species would quickly outgrow the space. Divide congested clumps in spring only when vigor declines.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; broader, paler leaflets than typical Cyrtomium fortunei, forming a substantial evergreen clump.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade. Sourced from a Sichuan Province population of Fortune's holly fern growing near 4,800 feet elevation, this selection has notably wider, lighter glossy-green leaflets that lack the dark central midrib typical of the species, giving it a softer, less contrasty look. It forms a full, substantial evergreen clump well suited to covering ground beneath shrubs or filling a large shaded container, and like other Cyrtomium fortunei selections resists deer and rabbit browsing and tolerates brief dry spells once rooted in.

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizome sections in spring after frost danger has passed, into consistently wet to saturated soil in partial sun to shade; spreads aggressively by long-creeping rhizomes and is best contained in a large pot or lined bed.

directions: Divide and plant rhizome sections in spring in consistently wet to saturated, humus-rich soil in partial sun to shade, where winters stay frost-free. Thelypteris interrupta is a pantropical wetland fern found from Florida and Mexico south to Argentina and across the Old World tropics, forming colonies of evergreen fronds along long, cord-like creeping rhizomes in marshes, ditches, and swamp margins. Its vigorous spreading habit makes it best suited to a bog garden, pond margin, or large contained planter rather than a mixed border, where it can run unchecked in warm, humid, waterlogged conditions. Give it steady humidity and year-round moisture; it will not tolerate drying out or hard frost.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)
